records.current_summary:
Rwanda demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, and the government formally tolerates a small LGBT presence — but a 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents ongoing law-enforcement abuses against transgender persons, including arbitrary arrests and detentions (framed as “vagrancy” or “deviance” round-ups in Kigali's periodic street-cleaning operations).

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but Kigali's sweep operations can net gender-nonconforming people, and recourse is nil. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and the constitution recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman — a partner-travel consideration for a trans visitor.

prison_adds.title: Rwanda's transgender community face violent detentions for being trans (VICE World News)
prison_adds.summary: VICE World News (20 Nov 2020): although being transgender is not criminalised in Rwanda, police routinely arrest trans women on pretext charges — 'homelessness', drug sales, theft — and detain them at Kigali's Gikondo Transit Center, a facility for people exhibiting 'deviant acts or behaviors'. Bella was held there after police falsely claimed she was homeless and sold drugs; as punishment she was confined in a tiny dark cell known as 'the cat box' and raped by fellow detainees at least three times. Gabi was detained at Gikondo for six months in 2018; Nunu was detained there three times between 2018 and 2019. Detainees are supposed to be charged within 72 hours or transferred to a police station, court, rehabilitation facility, or jail, but trans detainees are held for indeterminate periods in facilities lacking transparency. Documents placement practice: trans prisoners are held under a 'deviance rehabilitation' framework in transit centres (with segregated/confining cells used as punishment), not in facilities matching their gender identity.

prison_adds.title: Outright International: Rwanda country page
prison_adds.summary: Thin-to-useful: Outright's Rwanda page (updated March 2026, based on a July 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee) reports transgender individuals face heightened risks of harassment at identity checks and arbitrary arrests on grounds such as 'vagrancy' or 'public order' offenses, and that LGBTIQ people flee arbitrary arrests, detention and ill-treatment. It corroborates the detention pattern for trans people but gives no prison-placement (men's vs women's facility) detail.

records.current_summary:
Mali is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In October-November 2024 the Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code criminalising homosexuality for the first time — with the Justice Minister declaring that anyone “engaging in, promoting or apologising for” same-sex relations will be prosecuted; vague drafting suggests broad application, and prior “public indecency” provisions (Art 225) were already used against gender-nonconforming people. The junta context means no independent judiciary, no civil society space, and active conflict in much of the country.

For a visitor: a brand-new criminalisation statute under a junta with no recourse, plus conflict conditions.

prison_adds.title: World Report 2025: Mali — Human Rights Watch
prison_adds.summary: Thin: no usable prison-housing finding. The HRW World Report 2025 Mali chapter (Events of 2024) covers the junta's rule, counterterrorism sweeps (arbitrary arrest of 25 people in Ouro Fero village, Nara region) and an ICC arrest warrant, but contains no transgender-specific content and no information on prison placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners.

records.current_summary:
Haiti is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the national government has effectively collapsed: gangs control most of the capital (Port-au-Prince), the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition, no protection infrastructure, and no functioning judiciary.

The trans-specific risk is inseparable from the generalised collapse — outing in gang-controlled areas can be lethal. A 2018 official US State Department report described attitudes as hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity, particularly in the capital; freshness confirms trans people remain exposed to vagrancy-law fines with zero protection or hate-crime coverage.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Haiti - Wikipedia
prison_adds.summary: Thin for the prison-housing axis: the fetched article (HTTP 200) documents Haiti's legal framework - same-sex conduct legal since 1791, no legal gender-identity recognition, no anti-discrimination protections, and a June 2017 Senate bill penalising same-sex marriage with up to three years' imprisonment - plus documented harassment of transgender people in post-earthquake camps. It contains no prison-placement practice: no birth-sex-vs-identity housing rule, no trans special units, and no solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners; no usable placement finding.

records.current_summary: Nauru demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2016; tiny population (~12,000); no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; the asylum-detention legacy shaped its international image but not its LGBT law. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Nauru (Wikipedia) — Nauru Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014 gender-identity non-discrimination clause
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in Nauru article documents the only detention-related gender-identity provision found for Nauru: the Nauru Regional Processing Centre (RPC) Rules 2014, made under the Asylum Seekers (Regional Processing Centre) Act 2012, ban discrimination against any person based on sex or gender, sexual preference or gender identity within the RPC immigration-detention facility. This covers immigration detention, not Nauru's criminal-justice prison system, and concerns non-discrimination rather than placement by birth sex vs identity, special units, or solitary-confinement practice. No documented data was found on where transgender prisoners are housed in Nauru's corrections system, nor any trans-prisoner case or ruling.

records.current_summary: Grenada demands real caution. The buggery law (10 years) remains on the books (no successful court challenge yet), though unenforced; no LGR; small community; tourist areas insulated.

prison_adds.title: Grenada Stakeholder Report for the UN Universal Periodic Review: LGBTIQ+ Rights (The Advocates for Human Rights, Khaleem Ali, GrenCHAP)
prison_adds.summary: UN UPR stakeholder report (submitted 11 Oct 2024): because Grenada has no laws permitting legal gender change, 'the Government also prosecutes transgender women – who are considered legal men under the law.' The report provides no prison-specific housing/segregation detail, but it establishes the operative placement framework: a trans person's legal status, and so any correctional classification, follows registered/birth sex rather than gender identity. No special unit, solitary/segregation practice, or trans-prisoner housing case/ruling is documented for Grenada.

prison_adds.title: Grenada 2023 Human Rights Report (US State Dept)
prison_adds.summary: US State Dept 2023 report (pub. Feb 2024): Grenada's sole penitentiary, designed for about 200 persons, held 385 prisoners as of August 2023, including six women in a separate block; conditions were harsh due to gross overcrowding, with potable water in men's-block hallways but not cells. The report documents gendered blocks and general detention conditions but records no transgender-specific housing policy, special unit, or segregation practice, and no trans-prisoner cases or complaints.
